newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam says has plans to solve bank debt problems.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam says has plans to solve bank debt problems.

text.p: Vietnam's central bank chief said on Thursday steps would be taken to sort out problems faced by commercial banks which have issued deferred letters of credit, but gave no indication of how the debts would be covered.

"To solve the debt resulting from deferred letters of credit we have many measures," State Bank of Vietnam Governor Cao Si Kiem told reporters at a signing ceremony for a World Bank-funded road project.
"First of all, all commercial banks facing problems will classify their debts which relate to letters of credit and seek possible sources to balance and cover the debts," he said.
Asked if the central bank would use foreign currency reserves to help commercial banks meet their commitments, he replied: "It depends on the specific circumstances".
Economists say the stock of outstanding short-term debt in the banking system is at least $1.0 billion, much of it short-term letters of credit which are now falling due.
Concern about this debt was raised recently after a report that a prominent joint-stock bank had defaulted on a letter of credit and talk that many others had done the same.
When asked if the four big state-owned commercial banks would buy stakes in troubled joint-stock banks to bolster their capital, Kiem said that was a possibility.

There are more than 50 joint-stock banks, privately held institutions which have sprang up since the early 1990s. Unlike the state-owned banks, they cannot rely on the government to bail them out when trouble looms.

Kiem said the central bank had regulations in place already to solve problems such as guarantee risks, which would apply until new laws on the central bank and credit institutions are passed by the National Assembly in September or October.
Draft legislation was taken off the agenda of the National Assembly's spring session, which started on Wednesday, to give time for further improvements.
Kiem denied that the central bank had urged local journalists to cut back on coverage of the banking industry's problems.
"It's the journalists' right to cover or not...in conformity with the press law," he said.
